message.content:
A common example of a **multinucleated** cell is a *skeletal‑muscle fibre* (also called a **myocyte or myofiber**).  
During development several individual muscle precursor cells fuse together into one long cytoplasmic tube, leaving dozens—sometimes hundreds—to share a single contractile apparatus. Each nucleus remains distinct within this shared cytoplasm, so the resulting cell contains many nuclei side by side.

Other well‑known multinucleated cells include:

| Cell Type | Typical Function |
|-----------|------------------|
| Osteoclast | Bone-resorbing macrophage-derived cells – each has many nuclei to increase surface area for bone dissolution. |
| Trophoblast giant cells | Placental cells formed from fusion of trophoblast precursors; involved in nutrient transfer and hormone production during pregnancy. |
| Syncytium of certain fungal hyphae | Fungal filaments where nuclei move freely through continuous cytoplasm. |

So, when you hear “a cell with multiple nuclei,” think of skeletal‑muscle fibres as the classic human example.
